clue.text: Pallid Offa defiantly holds revolutionary national emblem (8)

indicators.note: What a thing holds is inside it, so these words are keeping a run of letters rather than being shuffled or abbreviated.
A revolutionary turns things round, so the run that has been found is read back the other way.

blocks.note: eight consecutive letters start inside the first word and stop inside the third

explanation.surface: A pale but defiant King Offa clutching some patriotic badge.
explanation.walkthrough: Offa was a Mercian king and 'pallid' keeps you in Anglo-Saxon England, which is the wrong country: the daffodil is the national emblem of Wales, worn on St David's Day.
explanation.definitionFit: The daffodil is the flower Wales adopts as its emblem, so 'national emblem' points at a plant rather than a flag or crest.

clue.text: Broadcast top recipe (3)

blocks.note: A1 means top quality, and the one in it is written as the Roman numeral
R is the R of an old prescription, from Latin recipe, 'take'

explanation.surface: A headline offering to share somebody's best recipe.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 comes from the shipping register's mark for a first-class vessel, and crosswords spell its one as I. Both halves here are conventions worth owning outright.
explanation.definitionFit: To air a programme is to put it out on radio or television, the verb sense broadcasters use every day.

clue.text: Cheeky underling returns to hotel (5)

indicators.note: Something that returns comes back the way it went, so the underling's letters are entered in the opposite order.

blocks.note: a SERF is a feudal underling, tied to the land, and here he is turned round
hotel is H in the international radio alphabet

explanation.surface: An impertinent junior being sent back to the hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheeky' is the informal adjective — being fresh with someone — while the surface reads the word as an errand. The serf is the medieval labourer, a crossword regular for a lowly worker.
explanation.definitionFit: To be fresh with someone is to be impertinent to them, so 'Cheeky' is that slangy adjective sense, not newly made.

clue.text: Part of DJ’s accompaniment? (5,5)

blocks.note: the reading the surface wants: the backing music a disc jockey puts on
the reading the setter meant: one item out of an outfit, because in Britain a DJ is a dinner jacket

explanation.surface: Somebody asking which bit of a disc jockey's backing music is meant.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a DJ is a dinner jacket as often as a disc jockey, and what goes with one is the stiff white dress shirt. There is no separable wordplay: the whole clue is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A dress shirt is the stiff-fronted white shirt worn with a dinner jacket, so it accompanies the DJ as part of the same outfit.

clue.text: Connect electric current in renovated aisle (6)

indicators.note: Renovating a building keeps every brick and rearranges them, which is exactly what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: five of the six letters, waiting to be reordered
I is the physicist's symbol for current, and it joins the shuffle

explanation.surface: Wiring being run through the aisle of a church that is being done up.
explanation.walkthrough: I for electric current comes up whenever a clue mentions amps or current, and it is worth learning once. 'Connect' here is the committee sense: to act as a go-between.
explanation.definitionFit: To liaise is to keep two parties in touch with each other, the go-between sense of 'Connect' rather than plugging anything in.

clue.text: Kind chap starts to lend encouragement (6)

indicators.note: A word's start is the letter it begins with, and the plural sense here takes one from each of the two words that follow.

blocks.note: a gent is a chap, short for gentleman
the first letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A kindly man beginning to offer a few words of support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kind chap' reads as a single description, which is the trap — only the first word is defining, and the chap belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A gentle manner is a kind one, so the adjective swaps straight in: gentle words, kind words.

clue.text: It’s part of playing American football, say (4)

indicators.note: Being part of something means sitting inside it, so the letters are already present, unbroken, in the words that follow.

blocks.note: four consecutive letters bridge the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: American football offered as an example of something you play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' marks a definition by example: the answer is the whole category and American football is one instance of it. 'Playing' is doing double duty, defining the surface and hiding the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: American football is one game among many, so 'say' flags a definition by example rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Signs from states encircling capitals of Oklahoma and Texas (9)

indicators.note: To encircle is to go round the outside, so the word for states opens up and takes the other piece within it.
The surface means capital cities, but a capital is also the big letter a name begins with — one from each name here.

blocks.note: states in the sense of sovereign countries; this is the piece that opens up
the initial letter of each name, slipped in after the first letter of the piece above

explanation.surface: Warnings coming out of American states that ring the capital cities of Oklahoma and Texas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capitals' is the trap: the clue wants capital letters, not Oklahoma City and Austin. 'Signs' is the written-symbol sense, the marks used in music or maths.
explanation.definitionFit: Notations are the systems of written symbols used in music, chess or maths, so 'Signs' means marks on a page.

clue.text: Finesse stage opening in England with finale of Tour tomorrow in France (11)

indicators.note: The opening of a word is the letter it begins with, so England contributes just the one.
A finale is the last thing to happen, so what is wanted is the closing letter of Tour.

blocks.note: a leg is a stage of a journey or a relay
the letter England opens with
the last letter of Tour
demain is French for tomorrow

explanation.surface: A cycling stage that starts in England, with the Tour's last day falling tomorrow in France.
explanation.walkthrough: Legerdemain is sleight of hand — literally 'light of hand' — so 'Finesse' is the conjuror's dexterity rather than a bridge player's play. The Tour de France really has begun in England, which is what makes the surface sit still.
explanation.definitionFit: Legerdemain is skilled trickery performed with the hands, and finesse is that same lightness of touch.

clue.text: Piece of cake and some cheeses, we’re told (6)

indicators.note: Being told something means hearing it, so the cheeses count for the noise they make and not for their spelling.

blocks.note: brie is the soft French cheese, and more than one of them are bries

explanation.surface: A cake and a cheeseboard being described to somebody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece of cake' is a phrase rather than a food, which is what the cheeseboard is there to disguise: both it and the answer mean something that takes no effort at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A breeze is anything achieved without effort, exactly what the idiom 'Piece of cake' means, so the two phrases swap as nouns.

clue.text: Lively Margate embraces independent poet (8)

indicators.note: Something lively will not stay still, so the town's letters refuse to keep the order they are given in.
To embrace is to take something in, so the extra letter is drawn into the shuffle rather than added on the end.

blocks.note: seven letters to be rearranged; Margate is a seaside town in Kent
I is the standard abbreviation for independent, as beside a candidate's name on a ballot

explanation.surface: A jolly seaside town taking in a writer who belongs to no party.
explanation.walkthrough: Simon Armitage has been Britain's Poet Laureate since 2019, so 'poet' defines him by example — and with no question mark to warn you that a single person is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Armitage is Simon Armitage, the Poet Laureate, so 'poet' names him as an instance of the category rather than as a synonym.

clue.text: Stress when preparing pie and mash before suppertime on vacation (9)

indicators.note: Preparing a dish chops and combines its ingredients, so the food arrives with its letters reordered.
This one is positional: the reordered food goes in front of what survives of suppertime.
A house on vacation stands empty, so suppertime loses everything between its two end letters.

blocks.note: seven letters to be reordered, the 'and' merely joining the dish together
the two end letters of suppertime, everything between them emptied out

explanation.surface: Someone cooking pie and mash ahead of an evening meal while away on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: Pie and mash is a London working-class dish, which is what makes the cooking surface hold together. 'Stress' is a verb here, not the noun of pressure the kitchen scene invites.
explanation.definitionFit: To emphasise a point is to stress it — the verb of underlining what matters, which both words share exactly.

clue.text: She distrusts everyone working in metaphors! (11)

definitions.note: The definition is a whole sentence rather than a noun: read it as 'one who distrusts everyone', which is the person the answer names.

indicators.note: Something working is being put through its paces, and letters put through their paces come out in a new order.

blocks.note: eleven letters, exactly the length the grid wants

explanation.surface: A suspicious woman who takes against everybody who talks in figures of speech.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark papers over the seam: 'in metaphors' is not part of the description at all but the letters themselves, the little word 'in' included.
explanation.definitionFit: A misanthrope distrusts and dislikes people in general, so 'everyone' is standing for the whole of humankind.

clue.text: Charge in transistor mechanism (5)

indicators.note: Here 'in' is meant literally: the letters sit inside the two words that follow, unbroken and in order.

blocks.note: five consecutive letters run across the join between the two words

explanation.surface: An electric charge somewhere inside the workings of a transistor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' is a verb here — troops storm a position — while the surface keeps your eye on electronics, where charge is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To storm a building is to charge at it in force, so 'Charge' is the verb of assault rather than anything electrical.

clue.text: Those intent on advancement air secrets ill-advisedly (10)

indicators.note: Doing a thing ill-advisedly is doing it wrongly, and letters set down wrongly are letters out of their proper order.

blocks.note: ten letters, matching the enumeration exactly

explanation.surface: Ambitious people leaking confidential information when they ought to keep quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air' wants to be the instruction — to air something is to broadcast it — but it is fodder, and the word doing the shuffling waits until the very end of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Careerists are people who put getting on ahead of everything else, so the plural definition names them by that ambition.

clue.text: Ignore trickery in speech (6)

indicators.note: What happens in speech is heard rather than written, so the trickery counts only for the sound it makes.

blocks.note: sleight, as in sleight of hand, is a conjuror's trickery

explanation.surface: Some deception being practised in the course of a conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words differ by one silent letter and sound identical, which is why setters love the pair. 'Ignore' is the verb of the snub: you slight someone by passing them over.
explanation.definitionFit: To slight a person is to snub them, deliberately taking no notice, which is the pointed sense of 'Ignore'.

clue.text: Tense, describing what was happening? (9)

blocks.note: the grammatical sense: one of the forms a verb can take
the job that tense does: reporting an action still going on in the past

explanation.surface: An anxious person giving an account of events as they unfolded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' reads first as nervous, and the second half quietly quotes itself: 'was happening' is written in the very tense the clue is defining, which is the setter's joke.
explanation.definitionFit: The imperfect is a verb tense, and it is the one used for an action in progress in the past — what was happening.

clue.text: Release standard expression of approval on the continent (6)

indicators.note: Continental Europe signals a foreign word, and the shout wanted here is the Spanish one.

blocks.note: par is the standard score set for a golf hole
olé is the shout of approval at a bullfight or a flamenco

explanation.surface: The usual roar of approval you would hear from a crowd somewhere in Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Release' is the noun the parole board grants — a prisoner let out on conditions — and PAR for standard is the golfer's word crosswords lean on constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: Parole is conditional release from prison, so 'Release' is the noun a prisoner is granted, not the act of freeing.

clue.text: Linen not available for every year (6)

blocks.note: NA is the shorthand a list uses for something not available
per means for each: fifty pence per person
y is the usual short form of year, as in 3y

explanation.surface: A shop reporting that its linen is out of stock for the whole year.
explanation.walkthrough: Napery is household table linen — cloths and napkins, from the same root as napkin — and it is built here out of three everyday abbreviations laid end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: Napery is the tablecloths and napkins a household keeps, so 'Linen' is the collective drapery sense rather than the fabric.

clue.text: A reed’s cultivated in area near Egypt (3,3)

indicators.note: Cultivating ground turns it over and breaks it up, and the letters given get the same treatment.

blocks.note: six letters, the s of the contraction counting as one of them

explanation.surface: A single reed being grown somewhere close to Egypt.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is fodder rather than a verb, which is the hard part: it quietly supplies the sixth letter while reading as 'a reed is'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Red Sea runs the length of Egypt's eastern coast, so the definition places the answer geographically instead of describing it.

clue.text: Employ in quiet place of study (6)

indicators.note: 'in' puts one piece within the other: the word for employ goes inside the word for quiet.

blocks.note: keeping mum is keeping quiet; this is the piece that opens up
to use something is to employ it

explanation.surface: Taking staff on in a hushed reading room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quiet place of study' reads as one phrase, and it sounds like a library — but only the last three words are the definition, and the first is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A museum keeps objects for scholars as well as visitors, the sense preserved in its Greek root mouseion, the hall of the Muses.

clue.text: Fastidious cleaner back from factory (5)

indicators.note: The back of a word is the letter it ends with, so factory gives up its final letter only.

blocks.note: a char is a domestic cleaner in Britain, short for charwoman
the last letter of factory

explanation.surface: A fussy cleaner coming home from a shift at the factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like a reversal instruction and is not — it asks for the final letter, and the surface's journey home is what sells the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: Chary means wary and careful about what one will accept, and that choosiness is the 'Fastidious' sense rather than tidiness.

clue.text: Reportedly fly staff in old aeroplane (9)

indicators.note: Something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the next word counts for its sound rather than its spelling.

blocks.note: to fly somewhere is to hurry, and it is the noise of the word that is wanted
a cane is a staff you walk with

explanation.surface: An urgent instruction to fly some employees out in a vintage plane.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hurricane was the RAF fighter that flew alongside the Spitfire in the Battle of Britain, so 'old aeroplane' names one particular machine.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hawker Hurricane is a Second World War fighter, so 'old aeroplane' defines the answer by example rather than by synonym.

clue.text: Regularly scour port city for unusual object (5)

indicators.note: Letters taken regularly come at a fixed interval, and the interval here is every second letter of the word that follows.

blocks.note: every second letter of scour: s-C-o-U-r
Rio de Janeiro is a Brazilian port, and its short name is a crossword staple

explanation.surface: Someone regularly combing a port city for something odd to buy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scour' is the wrong sort of searching: it is not telling you to hunt, it is handing over two of its own letters. The port city is a named one, not a general description.
explanation.definitionFit: A curio is a small object kept precisely because it is odd or rare, which is the curiosity 'unusual object' describes.

clue.text: Serenity derived from mathematical musings (4)

indicators.note: What is derived from something is taken out of it, so the letters come straight out of the words as written.

blocks.note: four consecutive letters straddle the space between the two words

explanation.surface: Peace of mind found in an afternoon of thinking about mathematics.
explanation.walkthrough: Hidden words hide best across a word break, and a long adjective like 'mathematical' is chosen to make you read for meaning instead of counting letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Calm is the noun for an untroubled state, and serenity is that same settled quiet, so the two swap as nouns.

clue.text: Uncontroversial fashion degree (8)

blocks.note: mode is fashion, as in à la mode
rate is the degree or extent at which something happens

explanation.surface: A safe, unremarkable university course in fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Degree' is the extent sense — the rate at which a thing runs — not a university qualification, which is where the fashion-course surface is pointing you.
explanation.definitionFit: A moderate view is a middle-of-the-road one that nobody takes offence at, which is what 'Uncontroversial' describes.

clue.text: Powerful ballad absorbs translator (6)

indicators.note: To absorb something is to take it right in, so the ballad closes over the two letters offered.

blocks.note: a ballad is a song; this is the piece that opens up
tr. is the standard abbreviation for translator on a title page

explanation.surface: A stirring ballad drawing in the person who is translating it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has the ballad absorbing someone emotionally while the wordplay has it swallowing two letters, and tr. is the title-page abbreviation worth keeping.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong wind or a strong argument is a powerful one, so the swap is the everyday adjective sense of force.

clue.text: On reflection, this sister doesn’t change (3)

indicators.note: A reflection is a mirror image, so the word is to be read from its far end as well as its near one.
Read the other way it comes out identical, which is the whole instruction: nothing turns into anything else.

blocks.note: the definition end of the clue: a woman in a religious order

explanation.surface: Second thoughts about a sister who never alters her ways.
explanation.walkthrough: NUN reads the same backwards, and 'doesn't change' is the setter saying so out loud. Nothing is turned into anything else, so there are no letters to hand over.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuns are addressed as Sister, so 'sister' names one by her religious title rather than by any family relation.

clue.text: Partition badly set up before beginning of meeting (6)

indicators.note: Something done badly comes out wrong, and letters set down wrong are letters out of order.
This one is positional: the reordered pair of words goes in front of the single letter that follows.
The beginning of a word is its first letter, so meeting contributes one letter and no more.

blocks.note: five letters waiting to be rearranged
the first letter of meeting

explanation.surface: A screen clumsily erected just before a meeting is due to start.
explanation.walkthrough: A septum is the wall of tissue dividing two cavities — the one in your nose is the familiar example — so 'Partition' is anatomical rather than a screen in an office.
explanation.definitionFit: A septum is the dividing wall between two chambers, in the nose or the heart, so it partitions a space in the body.

clue.text: Error when married nobleman loses head (8)

indicators.note: Losing your head means losing what sits on top, so the nobleman's first letter is the one that goes.

blocks.note: m is the standard abbreviation for married on a form
a VISCOUNT is a nobleman, and the V at his front is dropped

explanation.surface: A husband of noble birth losing his composure and getting something wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the beheading: a viscount, the rank just below an earl, literally loses his head here. 'Error' is a noun, so the answer has to be one too.
explanation.definitionFit: A miscount is a specific error, the mistake made in counting — the sort a returning officer orders a recount over.
